translations.title: Why can a position-controlled robot not execute a desired torque from WBC/TSID directly?
translations.answer: Desired torque is an upper-level dynamics result. High-ratio position-controlled joints still need calibrated sensing and inverse-dynamics estimation, platform identification, and bounded position offsets to map that torque into a validated actuator interface. HRP-2 identification cannot be copied to another robot or treated as equivalent to joint torque sensing.
translations.applicability.assumptions.0: External wrench sensing, IMU, and inertial model are calibrated for torque estimation.
translations.applicability.assumptions.1: The position-servo actuator map is identified and monitored over direction, speed, and temperature.
translations.applicability.environments.0: Model-based humanoid control on high-ratio position-controlled joints
translations.applicability.robots.0: HRP-2 in the paper; other position-controlled robots require independent identification
translations.applicability.simulators.0: Rigid-body dynamics models used for estimator and upper-level controller validation
translations.confidence_rationale: The paper provides an identified actuator model and HRP-2 trajectory/force experiments, while pinned TSID code confirms the separate upper-level inverse-dynamics layer. Confidence is capped because the low-level map is platform- and condition-specific and is not fully represented by modern TSID code.

translations.evidence.0.note: Shows the estimated torque-to-position-offset bridge and quantified HRP-2 tracking behavior.

translations.evidence.1.note: Confirms that TSID supplies upper-level task-space inverse dynamics rather than the paper's full HRP-2 estimator and actuator mapping.
